prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm interested in acquiring PlasticWorld, a plastic packaging manufacturer. PlasticWorld makes plastic packaging for beverages, cosmetics, household and automotive chemicals. Its products are top quality; it has 350 sets of molds with different materials, finishes, and colors, and the company is always innovating. The overall product mix has not changed in recent years. The sales force is considered best-in-breed and compensated on market share. Two years ago the company invested further in equipment for product innovation. PlasticWorld's customers exhibit strong loyalty but face increasing pressures in their industries to innovate their plastic packaging.
prompt.question: PlasticWorld's owners are requesting $25M. The offer is final. Should our client buy?

clarifying_info.q: How is the sales force compensated?
clarifying_info.a: Sales force is compensated based on market share.

clarifying_info.q: Are the products high quality and are customers loyal?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, products are top quality and customers are loyal — most would buy even at a higher price.

clarifying_info.q: Has the product mix changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: No, the overall product mix has not changed in recent years.
Two years ago the company invested in new equipment for product innovation, which raised depreciation.

clarifying_info.q: Can we see competitor profitability data?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — hand out Exhibit 2 at this point.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld P&L Statement (2007–2009)
exhibits.shows: Three-year income statement for PlasticWorld showing Sales ($), Volume (units), COGS ($), SG&A ($), Depreciation ($), and EBIT ($) for 2007, 2008, and 2009.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld and Industry Peers Profit Margins (%)
exhibits.shows: Horizontal bar chart comparing profit margin percentages for Competitor A through F and PlasticWorld. The x-axis runs from approximately -10% to +15%.
exhibits.data: Competitors A–F all show positive profit margins (roughly 5–12%). PlasticWorld shows a negative profit margin of approximately -6%.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld Valuation Sensitivity Analysis
exhibits.shows: Line chart showing company valuation ($M) on the y-axis (0–50) against profit margin (%) on the x-axis (-10 to +15), illustrating how valuation changes with profit margin.
exhibits.data: At 0% profit margin, valuation ≈ $25M. At the industry-average profit margin (~10%), valuation ≈ $40M. At -6% (current), valuation is well below $25M.

framework: 1. Understand current financial position: calculate revenue trend, volume trend, profit margin, and identify the root cause of the EBIT decline
2. Benchmark against industry: determine whether the profitability problem is company-specific or industry-wide
3. Valuation: use the sensitivity analysis to determine at what profit margin the company is worth $25M, and at what margin it exceeds $25M
4. Profit improvement levers: identify feasible operational changes that can raise profitability above the breakeven valuation threshold
5. Recommendation: synthesize whether the PE firm should buy at $25M given identified improvement opportunities

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1. What observations can you make from this P&L statement?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers three points: (1) Profit margin is negative and worsening — EBIT went from +$1.45M in 2007 to -$1.18M in 2009, implying a ~-6% margin on ~$19M revenue. (2) Sales volume is growing (32.75M → 36.2M units) while revenues are falling ($19.65M → $18.82M), which means the revenue drop is driven by falling prices, not volume loss. (3) Depreciation jumped from $2.25M to $3.45M between 2007 and 2008, reflecting the equipment investment; this is a one-time structural cost increase, not an operating deterioration.

questions.prompt: Given the volume is growing and product mix is unchanged, what is driving the revenue decline? What could explain the price drop?
questions.guidance: Prices are falling even though volume is up. Candidate should hypothesize: (a) competitive price pressure forcing discounts; or (b) internal incentive misalignment — the sales force is compensated on market share, giving them incentive to cut prices to win volume. Because products are high-quality and customers are loyal, competitive pressure alone does not justify price cuts; most customers would buy at higher prices. The sales force incentive (market share compensation) is the primary culprit.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, is this a company-specific or industry-wide problem?
questions.guidance: All competitors (A–F) have positive profit margins in the 5–12% range. PlasticWorld is the only player with a negative margin (~-6%). This confirms the problem is company-specific, not a sector-wide issue. Candidate should then ask: what realistic margin can PlasticWorld achieve? The industry average is a reasonable target (~10%).

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, what profit margin does PlasticWorld need to reach for the $25M offer to be fair? What would the company be worth at the industry average margin?
questions.guidance: From the valuation sensitivity curve: at 0% profit margin the company is worth ~$25M (the break-even point for the deal). At the industry average of ~10% profit margin the company would be worth ~$40M. The deal is attractive only if the PE firm believes it can realistically move the margin from -6% to at least 0%, and ideally toward the industry average.

math.setup: Read off the valuation chart: company value at various profit margin levels
steps: At 0% margin: company value ≈ $25M (equals the ask price)
math.answer: Break-even for the deal at 0% margin; upside of ~$40M at industry-average margins

questions.prompt: What specific changes could PlasticWorld make to improve profitability, and how feasible are they?
questions.guidance: Two main levers: (1) Change sales force compensation from market-share-based to earnings/profit-based — this is easy to implement and directly removes the incentive to cut prices; customers are loyal and quality is high so volume loss should be minimal. (2) Rationalize the product line — 350 molds is dense; eliminating lower-performing molds reduces material, storage, and changeover costs. Must be balanced against customer pressure to innovate. The PE firm should also examine other industry best practices for additional cost or revenue improvements.

brainstorming.prompt: What other areas or best practices should the PE firm examine to further improve PlasticWorld's profitability after the acquisition?

categories.name: Pricing & Revenue
ideas: Reprice products to reflect true quality premium
Introduce tiered pricing by customer segment
Renegotiate contracts with largest-volume customers to restore margin

categories.name: Sales Force & Incentives
ideas: Shift compensation to profit or earnings-based metrics immediately
Retain top performers with appropriate transition incentives
Train sales force on value-based selling

categories.name: Product Line Rationalization
ideas: Audit all 350 molds for revenue contribution and margin
Focus innovation budget on highest-demand packaging categories
Co-develop next-generation packaging with key loyal customers

categories.name: Cost Structure
ideas: Benchmark COGS against industry peers and identify procurement savings
Review depreciation schedule for any accelerated write-offs that can normalize

categories.name: Customer Strategy
ideas: Deepen relationships with loyal customers to lock in multi-year contracts
Offer innovation partnership programs to meet customers' packaging innovation needs without proliferating SKUs
Segment customers by strategic value and protect top accounts

recommendation: Accept the $25M offer — the deal is at break-even valuation today but has clear upside if margins are improved even modestly
Immediately change sales force compensation from market-share-based to profit/earnings-based to remove the pricing incentive distortion
Rationalize the 350-mold product line to cut costs while using the strong sales force to maintain customer satisfaction
risks: Sales force resistance or attrition when compensation structure changes
Customer churn if price increases are not carefully managed despite high loyalty
Innovation pipeline gaps if too many molds are cut, given customer pressure to innovate packaging
next_steps: Conduct detailed due diligence on sales force contracts and compensation re-structuring feasibility
Model the impact of eliminating specific mold sets on revenue and cost
Benchmark PlasticWorld's operations against industry peers to identify additional cost-reduction opportunities
Develop a 100-day post-acquisition plan focused on compensation reform and SKU rationalization
